title: Will the Moment You ‘Make It’ Be the Moment You Start Falling Behind?
author: Joel Salinas
summary: Salinas argues that success, not failure, is the greater threat to a leader's growth because it breeds the belief that learning is finished. After a win, rest slides into autopilot, feedback gives way to affirmation, and leaders do more of what they are already good at. Drawing on Maxwell and Goldsmith, and on his own habit of learning unrelated skills such as juggling, latte art and chess, he insists that arrival is a myth and coasting is drift. He extends the point to mission-driven work, where a leader running on past growth cannot pour vision into others. He closes with three concrete practices: list books, name two skills to develop, and block time to learn something random.
points: Success is the real hazard to growth because it signals leaders to coast, stop seeking feedback and avoid risk.
Quoting Goldsmith, what got you here will not get you there, so leaders must keep letting go of what worked and of ego.
Pursuing non-strategic skills keeps a leader curious and humble, which Salinas treats as a leadership discipline.
In mission-driven organisations the messenger matters as much as the mission, so a leader who stops learning cannot lead others.
Three small habits keep growth going: a reading list, two target skills, and ninety protected minutes of random learning.
quotes: But there’s a quiet danger waiting just after we hit a new milestone, when the applause fades, the inbox quiets, and you go to bed at night telling yourself: “I’ve made it.” That may come at the first big-paying job, or first house purchase, or first senior leadership position, or reaching 10K subscribers.
Most people assume failure is the great threat to growth. It’s not. I’d argue success is.
The moment I start protecting what I already know, I know I’m in danger of becoming stagnant.
But what begins as rest often slides into autopilot. And over time, autopilot slides into irrelevance.
If we want to keep growing, we have to keep letting go of what worked, of what’s safe, of our own ego. Because the truth is: arrival is a myth.

You can’t pour vision into others if you’re running on the fumes of past growth. You can’t keep doing what you do successfully if you’re no longer learning anything new, if you are not adding fuel to your engine.
The people I trust most aren’t the ones with the best résumés. They’re the ones who keep learning when no one’s making them.
